Every morning we would join a class with other students. We could see their names on their screen, and we could interact with them before and after class. As "learning coach", I supervised their studies through the rest of the day, each day.

Children need social time, so field trips were planned, where the other home schooled kids---the names we saw on the side of the screen---would show up. The school planned some, but they encouraged parents to set up field trips for the students as well. Lots of really nice people. All felt they were doing right for their kids and the next generation.

Where we lived, k12 was considered a Title 1 school, just like a regular brick-and-mortar school building. The kids still had to do state testing each spring. We would get together with the same kids we went on field trips with at a proctored location, and the kids would fill in the circles. k12 students always scored high.

The whole platform worked around proper study skills. It taught kids the joy of learning from kindergarten. And it helped that my kids had a beautiful natural sibling rivalry.

Children can advance at their own speed. My youngest was in k while my oldest was in 1st. During his 4th grade year, he knocked out the 5th grade material as well, so I thankfully only had to give one lesson a day rather than two after that.

This was during the era just before the common core shit, so I don't know if k12 got into that. I recall the US History textbook questioning the Gulf of Tonkin bullshit, and some other historical myths. And as a good father should, I was there to guide them through other questions like WW2 and 9/11.

When we finally moved to a good school district (good, meaning "no diversity", and in the top 5% in the state) I let them attend public school. They knocked out advanced courses through high school, and both graduated at the top of the class.
That is great. I'm glad it worked out for you and your kids.

It's not an online answer, but kids need to also experience the physical part of the world as well.

Making things, crafting things, building things, experimenting - and experiencing what works and what doesn't for themselves.

Getting off of the screen and using real world materials and tools is (even simple stuff) is powerful.
